source_style: supplier shipment / price sheet exported from Excel under a European (decimal-comma) locale

clean_table.description: After cleaning: split on ';' (NOT ','), strip the UTF-8 BOM from the first header cell ('ShipmentID', not '\ufeffShipmentID'), then for Quantity_kg/UnitPrice_EUR_per_kg/Yield_Percent strip '.' thousands separators and replace ',' with '.' before casting to float (e.g. '1.279,2' -> 1279.2, '12,75' -> 12.75, '98,1' -> 98.1). DeliveryDate parsed as dd.mm.yyyy. 27 data rows, no missing values in ShipmentID/Supplier/Material/Quantity/UnitPrice/Yield/DeliveryDate; Notes has 14 blanks.
clean_table.structure: One row per ShipmentID (SH2026-001..SH2026-027), no repeats or nesting.

intended_analysis: Track raw-material cost per kg and delivered yield by supplier/material over time to negotiate future contracts.
mess_applied: semicolon-delimited instead of comma-delimited (forced by the European decimal-comma Excel locale that produced the file)
UTF-8 encoded WITH a byte-order mark (BOM) prepended
Quantity_kg, UnitPrice_EUR_per_kg, and Yield_Percent all written with European decimal-comma convention; Quantity_kg additionally uses '.' as a thousands separator above 1000 kg
DeliveryDate is text in dd.mm.yyyy order
what_a_naive_reader_would_get_wrong: A CSV reader that assumes the default comma delimiter (never checking for ';') would shred every numeric field at its decimal comma into two bogus columns -- e.g. 'ShipmentID;Supplier;Material;Quantity_kg;...' parsed on ',' produces a single one-column row per line, and a line like the 'Tereos France SA;Lactose;1.279,2;1,23;98,1;...' row would instead split '1.279,2' into '1.279' and '2' as separate fields if it guessed ',' as the delimiter, corrupting every column downstream. A reader that doesn't decode with utf-8-sig (or strip the BOM) will see the first header as '\ufeffShipmentID', which fails to match a lookup for 'ShipmentID' and silently drops/renames the first column. Even once the delimiter and BOM are handled correctly, naively casting the numeric text columns with a US-locale float parser will mis-parse '1.279,2' (thousands dot + decimal comma) as 1.279 or throw, and misparse '12,75' as 1275 if the comma is stripped as a thousands separator instead of a decimal mark.
